evaluation.positioning_hook: A bullied teen discovers she can copy anyone she touches — then learns she’s actually a brain-wiped shapeshifter trapped in a biotech cover-up, with a billionaire’s body on the line.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and built for broad genre curiosity: a teen identity story, a cover-up, and a body-swapping engine that keeps escalating from school to mall to secret lab. The Ava/Madison reveal and the billionaire endgame give it a clean commercial promise that can travel well with the right cast and trailer.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the opening chase and then sharpens through the roadside reveal, the school confrontation, and the final identity reversal. The story engine is easy to explain in one breath: touch someone, become them, and survive the people who made you.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ava/Madison has a strong emotional contradiction — smart, self-doubting, morally stubborn — and June gives the story a sharp, blue-collar maternal counterweight. The supporting players are functional and vivid in the moment, though the script is most alive when it stays locked on the Ava/Madison/June triangle.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The shapeshifting is not just a gimmick here; it becomes a device for class, identity, memory, and self-worth, especially in the Ava-Christy, Ava-Grandma, and Ava-Eric transformations. The script keeps finding fresh dramatic uses for the same power set, which gives it a confident, writerly stamp.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps turning the screw: roadside chase, school intrusion, first transformation, reveal of the company, the mistaken identity collapse, and the lab showdown all arrive with forward charge. Even the quieter scenes are doing engine work, because every conversation is carrying new information or a new identity test.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a girl who thinks she is Ava but is actually Madison, with memory contamination from the foam, gives the premise a memorable emotional and conceptual twist. The final reveal reframes everything in a way that feels surprising but seeded, which is exactly the kind of originality that sticks.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The town, school, mall, and secret lab all feel like parts of one social ecosystem, with company SUVs, school authority, local rumor, and private security creating a believable pressure field. The world is strongest when it stays grounded in the town’s institutions and the company’s quiet takeover.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone blends teen awkwardness, body-horror panic, and corporate paranoia in a way that feels specific rather than generic. Scenes like the burger joint crush, the mall disguise sequence, and the lab meltdown give the script a distinct mix of sincerity and freakout energy.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the thriller surface, the script is really about self-contempt, class shame, maternal love, and the hunger to be seen, and those themes deepen as the identity swaps accumulate. The Ava note to Madison and the final found-family turn suggest a larger emotional life beneath the genre machinery.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Ava-June-Shannon triangle has real story energy, and Madison/David adds a compelling bond once the reveal lands. Beyond that core, the supporting cast mostly serves the chase and the conspiracy, so the script plays more as a strong lead-driven feature than a full ensemble engine.

casting_characteristics: One child performer required for Madison in the opening and later reveal
Multiple identity/body-shift performances for the same core roles
Teen casting for Ava, Shannon, Liam, and Christy
Adult roles with strong authority presence for June, Priscilla, Wolcott, Jamieson, Mills, Wilma, and David

notable_requirements: High school interiors and exterior parking lot
Mall concourse, bathrooms, and Target-style retail spaces
Contained secret lab / warehouse / conference room / morgue build
Suburban house interiors and a townhouse safe house

technical.vfx_details: Frequent body-shift transformations, skin bubbling/mutation effects, fire and explosion beats, and some digital enhancement for the shapeshifter reveals.
technical.sfx_needs: Foam spray effects, electrical discharge, fire ignition, gunfire, tasers/cattle prods, practical burns, and lab destruction.

rights_flags.detail: Eric Huntington is a fictionalized billionaire figure, but the script references New York Times as a plot device and names public institutions like CNN.
Trader Joe’s, Target, iPhone, Google Docs, CNN, TikTok, and Ford/Honda are referenced on the page.
No plot-critical named music is referenced.
Indiana Jones is referenced in dialogue.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Streaming feature or festival-to-platform genre lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with strong trailerable hook and genre-festival upside, then platform-friendly genre rollout.

cost.note: The story is mostly contained, but the repeated transformation effects, lab destruction, and action beats push it above a micro-budget lane.

cast.note: The core cast is manageable, but the project depends on precise teen casting and convincing body-swap performances across several identities.

location.note: It moves through a town, school, mall, homes, woods, and a secret lab, but the footprint stays within a single community.

content.note: Violence, body horror, child endangerment, and torture imagery are present, but the script stays below explicit adult-content territory.

rights.note: The script uses mostly generic or easily clearable references, with a few brand and pop-culture mentions that are straightforward to address.

strengths.what_it_means: This has the kind of clean, high-concept engine that can sell in a sentence and cut into a strong teaser: a teen body-swaps through touch, then discovers the whole identity is a lie. That makes it attractive to genre buyers who want a hook audiences can grasp immediately and repeat to friends.
strengths.evidence: The opening chase, the roadside shapeshift reveal, and the later discovery that Ava is really Madison.

strengths.what_it_means: The script turns body-swapping into plot propulsion, not just a visual effect, which gives the movie a built-in escalation pattern and a fresh way to stage pursuit, disguise, and revelation. That is catnip for buyers looking for a genre piece with a clear gimmick that also carries emotional stakes.
strengths.evidence: Ava becomes Christy, Grandma, Eric, and multiple other bodies to evade capture and survive the lab.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The emotional core is a mother-daughter bond.
strengths.what_it_means: June is not just support; she becomes the story’s moral and survival anchor, which broadens the movie beyond a teen thriller into a family-driven genre play. That gives the project a stronger emotional runway for actors and for buyers who want genre with heart.
strengths.evidence: June’s car escape, the mall disguise sequence, and the final alliance between June, Real Ava, and Madison.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The teen world feels current and specific.
strengths.what_it_means: The high school, social media, TikTok slop, crush dynamics, and class-room authority scenes make the movie feel rooted in a recognizable now, which helps the concept land with younger audiences without losing older viewers. That contemporary texture is useful for streamers and genre labels looking for something current rather than nostalgic.
strengths.evidence: The school scenes, the AI-slop videos, the cafeteria gossip, and the Liam/Christy/Ava triangle.

strengths.what_it_means: This is not a faceless monster movie; it’s a biotech cover-up with private security, investors, lawyers, and a billionaire endgame, which gives the story a commercial conspiracy flavor. Buyers who like institutional paranoia and clean antagonistic systems will see a lot to work with here.
strengths.evidence: Priscilla, Wolcott, Jamieson, the investors, the lab, and the Eric Huntington money play.

strengths.what_it_means: Each body change is a chance for an actor to play a different social register, age, class, and emotional state inside one role, which is exactly the kind of showcase that gets reps and casting directors excited. That makes the project especially magnetic to actors who want a role with range rather than a single-note genre part.
strengths.evidence: Ava-Christy, Ava-Grandma, Ava-Eric, Madison-Eric, and David-Priscilla all function as distinct performance modes.

whats_special.headline: This is a sharp, commercial sci-fi thriller with a real emotional spine: a teen identity story that keeps mutating into a conspiracy movie, a body-horror chase, and a mother-daughter survival drama. The concept is easy to sell, the transformations are actor bait, and the final reveal gives the whole thing a memorable aftertaste.

lead_characters.name: Ava / Madison
lead_characters.hook: Ava presents as a bright, self-conscious small-town teen with a sharp mouth and a private ache to be seen, but the script keeps peeling her open until she becomes Madison, the frightened child at the center of the experiment. She is funny, observant, morally stubborn, and emotionally porous in a way that makes every identity shift feel like both a power-up and a wound.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Saoirse Ronan in 'Lady Bird' colliding with Toni Collette in 'Hereditary' — a role that lets an actor play teenage insecurity, body panic, and moral awakening in one arc. Young actresses looking for a prestige breakout will chase this because it offers comedy, fear, transformation, and a final emotional reveal that redefines the whole performance.

lead_characters.name: June
lead_characters.hook: June is a blue-collar, fast-talking, tattooed single mom who feels like she’s been forced to improvise adulthood in real time, and the script makes her both comic and formidable. She’s the kind of mother who can joke through chaos, steal a car, and still land the emotional truth of a scene in one line.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Frances McDormand in 'Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri' — a woman whose toughness is inseparable from grief, wit, and love. Mid-career actresses who want a role with authority, humor, and action-forward maternal energy will see this as a juicy lead part.

lead_characters.name: Shannon
lead_characters.hook: Shannon is Ava’s blunt, loyal best friend, the kind of teen who can puncture delusion with one line and still stay emotionally available when things get real. She gives the movie its grounded peer perspective and keeps the story from floating away from ordinary teenage life.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of best-friend showcase that Beanie Feldstein had in 'Booksmart' — a role built on timing, warmth, and the ability to make exposition feel lived-in. Young comedic actresses who want a scene-stealing supporting lead will be drawn to the part because Shannon gets to be funny, skeptical, and emotionally essential.

lead_characters.name: Priscilla
lead_characters.hook: Priscilla is the polished, hard-edged face of the company: calm, strategic, and capable of sounding reasonable while doing monstrous things. She’s not a cartoon villain; she’s a corporate operator who understands optics, leverage, and how to speak to frightened people.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of icy authority role that Sarah Snook had in 'Succession' — a character who can weaponize intelligence, poise, and menace in the same breath. Character actresses who like playing controlled power will chase it because Priscilla gets to dominate rooms without raising her voice.

lead_characters.name: Wilma
lead_characters.hook: Wilma is the most human face inside the machine, a young company nurse whose empathy makes her feel like a possible ally until the script reveals how deeply she’s implicated. She carries a quiet, unsettling duality: compassionate on the surface, complicit underneath.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of morally split role that Elisabeth Moss often gets in prestige thrillers — someone who can play sincerity, fear, and hidden allegiance in the same scene. Actors who want a part with emotional ambiguity and a late-story shock turn will be interested.

lead_characters.name: Jamieson
lead_characters.hook: Jamieson is the blunt instrument of the operation, a security man whose job is to enforce the lie and keep the chaos contained. He’s physically imposing, procedural, and just self-aware enough to feel like a real employee of a rotten system.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of hard-edged enforcer role that Walton Goggins has played in 'Justified' and 'The Shield' — a part that lets an actor bring menace, fatigue, and dry humor to a functionally dangerous character. Character actors who like playing pressure-cooker authority will want it.

lead_characters.name: Mills
lead_characters.hook: Mills is the soldier in the room who still has a conscience, and the script uses him as the one company man who can be shaken by what he’s helping do. He reads as practical, exhausted, and increasingly trapped between orders and decency.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of conflicted lawman-adjacent role that Jesse Plemons has made compelling in 'Fargo' and 'Breaking Bad' — a man whose quiet face can carry a whole moral collapse. Actors who specialize in internal pressure and late-breaking conscience will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Wolcott
lead_characters.hook: Wolcott is the cold scientist-architect of the whole nightmare, a man who talks about vision while treating people like material. He has the clipped certainty of someone who believes history will forgive him because he thinks he’s building the future.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of prestige-villain role that Bryan Cranston had in 'Breaking Bad' once the mask fully came off — a character whose intelligence and self-justification are the performance. Veteran actors who want a clean, chilling antagonist with monologue space will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: David
lead_characters.hook: David is the other shapeshifter, and the script makes him tragic, unstable, and deeply dependent on connection. He’s the emotional mirror to Madison: damaged, loving, manipulative, and desperate to survive inside whatever body he can hold onto.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of fractured identity role that James McAvoy had in 'Split' — a performance slot built around rapid shifts, emotional volatility, and the challenge of making multiple selves feel like one wounded person. Actors who want a technically demanding, high-wire part will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Liam
lead_characters.hook: Liam starts as the crush-object dreamboat and then becomes one of the story’s most unnerving identity clues, which gives him a strange, slippery charge. He’s sweet, athletic, and hard to read, which makes every appearance feel slightly off-kilter once the shapeshifter logic kicks in.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of deceptively simple teen role that Timothée Chalamet had in 'Call Me by Your Name' before the emotional complexity blooms — a part that lets an actor play charm, mystery, and later dread. Young actors with leading-man potential will like the mix of romance and genre unease.

lead_characters.name: Christy
lead_characters.hook: Christy is the polished teen ideal Ava thinks she can never be: tall, athletic, socially effortless, and apparently untouchable. The script uses her as both a social rival and a body template, which makes her more than a mean-girl placeholder.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of glossy teen role that Rachel McAdams had in 'Mean Girls' — a part that can be iconic because it defines the social hierarchy of the movie. Young actresses who want a memorable, image-forward supporting role will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Eric Huntington
lead_characters.hook: Eric is the dead billionaire whose body becomes the ultimate prize, and even in limited screen time he reads as vain, entitled, and structurally central to the conspiracy. He functions as the face of wealth, power, and the fantasy of total reinvention.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-stage power role that Michael Keaton had in 'The Founder' — a man whose charisma and entitlement are the engine of the system around him. Name actors who like playing polished, morally rotten power will be interested even in a contained role.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make body horror feel emotional, not just grotesque.
director_appeal.fit_profile: First- or second-feature directors, or established indie genre directors, who already work in performance-forward thrillers and know how to stage tension without overrelying on spectacle. This material rewards directors who care about identity, social pressure, and visualizing internal panic through clean, escalating set pieces.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a chance to choreograph transformations as character beats, not effects beats, and to move from teen realism into lab-nightmare territory without losing emotional coherence. It will attract filmmakers who want a contained but ambitious genre feature with room for strong actors and a distinctive visual language.

buyer_appeal.lane: Streaming genre feature / festival-to-platform sci-fi thriller
buyer_appeal.detail: The cast can be anchored by one breakout teen lead and one strong adult mother role, so it does not require a giant ensemble or multiple name attachments to make sense on paper. The contained-town footprint, trailer-friendly hook, and body-swap conceit fit the current buyer appetite for elevated genre that can launch on a streamer or through festival discovery.

considerations.area: The Ava/Madison reveal carries the whole movie.
considerations.detail: The final identity turn is the script’s biggest emotional and conceptual payoff, so the next pass could keep seeding Madison’s interior life a little earlier in the middle stretch. A few more moments where the audience feels the child beneath Ava would make the ending land with even more force.

considerations.area: The middle leans heavily on explanation scenes.
considerations.detail: The conference-room disclosures with Priscilla, Wilma, and later David do important work, but they are also the places where the movie pauses to define the rules. One direction would be to let a little more of that information arrive through action or contradiction so the momentum keeps its grip while the mythology clarifies.

considerations.area: The body-swap rules are rich enough to simplify.
considerations.detail: The script currently tracks several identities, memory states, and body forms across Ava, Madison, David, June, Eric, Priscilla, and others. A cleaner version of the same story could collapse one or two of the late-stage identity permutations without losing the core emotional turn, which would make the climax easier to follow and cheaper to stage.

considerations.area: The teen triangle could carry more story weight.
considerations.detail: Ava, Shannon, Liam, and Christy all have useful screen presence, but the script mostly uses them as pressure points around the main plot. There is room for one more scene or beat where the friendship or crush dynamic changes the stakes in a way that matters to the conspiracy, which would deepen the teen-world engine.

The secret-lab destruction, fire, foam, and multiple transformations make the climax feel big and cinematic, but they also concentrate the effects load at the end. A version that keeps the same emotional outcome while trimming one transformation beat or one destruction beat would protect the spectacle and keep the finale nimble.
